title: RCC RefCert: A Research Toolkit for Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity
description:
RCC RefCert is an open-source toolkit for studying quantum circuit complexity. Given the parameters of your preparation model, you can compute a rigorous lower bound on optimal quantum circuit complexity from final-state data. Use an exact spectrum, fixed-effect counts or a complete projective readout collected under a prespecified protocol.

You can build your own quantum models and compare preparation strategies. With a density matrix, you can study which structures appear locally and which arise from correlations in a pure or mixed state. Share the model, inputs and results for independent verification.

The toolkit is based on Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC), introduced by Liu, Tian and Wu in Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity: An Auditable Information-Theoretic Lower Bound.

Features of reference-contingent complexity

Structural fairness makes circuit complexity comparable across physical settings

Quantum circuit complexity is often measured by the minimum number of gates needed to prepare a target state from a fixed initial state. Counting starts once the inputs are ready, so equal gate counts can conceal different physical costs. For example, one device may supply a pure ancillary qubit, while another must first reset a qubit in a mixed state to obtain one. Structural fairness is RCC's physical postulate for making this distinction. Before choosing the target, fix what the background supplies, the available controls, their costs and the weights assigned to control programs. The background sets the reference zero point. A preparation pays for the resources it uses, even for a step that preserves global entropy. To carry a bound from one setting to another, account for the change of reference and the cost and accuracy of translating the controls.

Final-state data give a rigorous lower bound on optimal circuit complexity

With the model, cost rules and required accuracy fixed, optimal quantum circuit complexity is the infimum of the costs of all circuits that successfully prepare the target. Why can a measurement on the target rule out cheaper circuits? The model's transcription bound gives every low-cost circuit a short control description. Short descriptions carry greater weight in the mixture of program outputs, and the reference certificate bounds that whole mixture. An outcome that is common in the target yet rare under the reference can therefore rule out every circuit below a calculable cost, even after allowing for preparation error.

Research tasks

  • Study graph-state measurements and cooling programs. With the default synthetic data, each color setting certifies at least one slot of preparation cost. Combining the two raises the lower bound to two slots. The three-qubit cooling study asks which programs reach the full target within tolerance and how joint measurements resolve target polarization and correlations with the bath.
  • Plan a fixed-size acquisition. Choose a response or cost threshold, plan how many trials to collect and use the target and reference counts to calculate a lower bound.
  • Build a finite-control model for RCC certification. Describe your setup in terms of its reference state, available quantum channels and control rules. Once you verify its reference bound, you can use that bound for different targets in the same model.
  • Certify a lower bound on optimal circuit complexity. Rule out circuits below the certified cost for the specified target and tolerance. Use an exact target spectrum or fixed-projector measurement counts at a prespecified confidence level. The worked example goes from a model certificate to a cost bound.
  • Compare preparation strategies. See which programs reach your target within tolerance and what each one costs. For exact diagonal-preserving models, the cyclic-reset and algorithmic-cooling examples show when the bounds establish the optimum and when a gap remains.
  • Analyze pure-state complexity with window RCC. Compare pure states with the same global RCC value by the structure visible in their subsystems and correlations. The same window analysis applies to mixed states. With your own density matrices, you can separate local and correlation contributions and track how each changes during preparation.
  • Share a calculation for independent verification. Send a colleague one bundle containing the original inputs and results so they can recompute and verify the calculation independently.
  • Reproduce the paper's reference calculations. Run python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check to reproduce the bundled cases. Three MATCH results confirm agreement with the frozen expectations, data and report. The paper-to-code map connects the cases to the paper's equations.

Run and share a calculation

With Python 3.10 or newer, install the package and run the four-qubit reset task in a new working directory.

python -m pip install "rcc-refcert==0.4.0"
python -m rcc_refcert cost template cyclic-reset > task.json
python -m rcc_refcert cost analyze task.json --bundle task.rccbundle

At the default trace-distance tolerance of 1/10, the result is [5,5] atomic slots. The model rules out shorter programs, and a five-slot program reaches the target with halt included. Change epsilon in task.json to try another tolerance and choose a new bundle filename for the next run. Verify the saved calculation with the following command.

python -m rcc_refcert bundle verify task.rccbundle

Interpreting the results

Exact diagonal-preserving models can bracket the optimal preparation cost between a rigorous lower bound and the cost of a successful program. For general matrix models, the numerical checks give each candidate's cost and trace distance from the target. Window RCC compares state-side complexity at a fixed reference and control bandwidth. A finite-accuracy lower bound on preparation cost also uses the model parameters and one-shot corrections. The scientific scope explains the quantities and their units.
notes: If you use this software in your research, please cite the software version used and the associated RCC paper.
